chunks: Asynchronous versus synchronous communication. The question: What is the difference between asynchronous vs synchronous communication? What are the tradeoffs?
Every receiver must decide when to read each bit. Synchronous links, like SPI and I2C, send a clock along with the data, and the receiver reads on the clock's tick.
Asynchronous links, like UART, have no clock wire.
Both sides agree on a speed beforehand, a start bit marks the beginning of each byte, and the receiver counts time with its own clock.
Picture two rowers. In the synchronous case, a coach beats a drum and both follow it, so they stay together at any speed. In the asynchronous case, there is no drum.
Each wears a watch, they start on the same signal, and each counts strokes by their own watch.
If the watches differ a little, they stay together briefly and drift apart over a long stretch. That is why asynchronous bytes are short, and each starts with a fresh signal.
Synchronous. Data changes at falling clock edges and is sampled at the rising edges (vertical lines).
Setup and hold are naturally half a clock period each, and if the clock slows down the data slows down with it. The sampling point is tied to the data by construction.
Synchronous: sender and receiver share a clock, and bits are read on its ticks ("I2C, SPI and UART: how each works"). Asynchronous: no shared clock.
The receiver times each bit with its own oscillator. Baud rate: the agreed number of bits per second on an asynchronous line.
Start and stop bit: extra bits framing each asynchronous byte, a 0 at the start and a 1 at the end. Oscillator: the circuit that makes a chip's clock tick.
Quartz-crystal ones are accurate; cheap built-in ones drift.
A common UART byte (8N1) is 1 start bit, 8 data bits and 1 stop bit, 10 bits in all, so only 80% are data. The receiver reads the last bit 9. 5 bit lengths after the byte begins.
If its clock runs 5% fast, it reads 9. 5 times 0. 05 = 0. 475 of a bit early, almost half a bit, so it is near failing. The limit is 0. 5 over 9. 5 about 5. 3 % .
That is the whole idea.
"Synchronous means the sender and receiver share a clock, so the receiver samples on that clock's edge. SPI and I2C work this way.
It's fast and low overhead but costs a clock wire and has setup and hold timing to meet.
Asynchronous, like UART, has no clock wire: both sides agree on a baud rate, a start bit resynchronizes the receiver, and it samples each bit with its own clock.
That saves a wire but adds about 20% overhead and needs both clocks within a few percent."
